article.title: US suspends military cooperation with Ecuador amid human rights violations probe
article.author: BreakThrough News
article.content: The US government announced a move that has surprised many in Ecuador. For several weeks, Washington and Quito have been touting, through press releases, various military and intelligence operations against organized crime in Ecuador. According to several media outlets , including The Atlantic and The New York Times , the US has decided to suspend these joint operations until it clarifies incidents in which abuses and killings may have been committed against suspects in custody of Ecuadorian forces on September 23 . According to US media reports , Washington wants to determine whether Carlos Muñoz, alias “Charlie” – one of the leaders of Los Choneros, one of Ecuador’s most prominent criminal gangs – along with other suspects, was killed while in custody. On September 23, Ecuador’s Minister of Defense, Gian Carlo Loffredo, released images showing a man believed to be alias “Charlie” and other dead bodies lying in a bloody mess alongside weapons in a pickup truck. In a post on X, Loffredo says : “Alias ‘Charlie’ belonged to the Los Choneros and Frente Oliver Sinisterra groups in Colombia, had ties to Mexico’s Jalisco New Generation Cartel, and his main mission was to sow terror in our country.” Read more: ‘They laughed at what they had done’: Ecuadorian fishermen sue US after surviving drone strike at sea In addition, Loffredo added : “The Ecuadorian Armed Forces, in cooperation with US Southern Command within the framework of the Internal Armed Conflict, have eliminated one of the highest-value military targets on Ecuadorian soil… We promised: ‘Prison or hell,’ and this one didn’t make it to prison.” The alleged investigation is also seeking to determine whether US military personnel participated in the operation. However, the Times clarified that the US Department of Defense issued a statement saying that no US soldier participated in the alleged crimes and that the Trump administration “[takes] allegations of misconduct by our partners seriously.” This incident comes just one week after Pete Hegseth visited Quito and held a meeting with Ecuador’s president, the right-wing Daniel Noboa, who is currently in the midst of a local election campaign. A few days ago, several Ecuadorian fishermen filed a complaint against the Trump administration for allegedly bombing their boat on the high seas and detaining them before sending them against their will to El Salvador. Two fishermen were injured in the attack. A major setback for the Noboa administration Despite repeated promises, Noboa’s government has failed to halt the worst wave of violence in the country’s history, which has so far claimed thousands of lives. Instead, it found a boost to its security policy – based on a quasi-perpetual state of emergency – in US military and logistical support. The news comes just days before local elections in which Ecuador will elect 24 prefects, 221 mayors, and hundreds of council members and local government board members. Noboa has led the election campaign in support of his party’s candidates. He has not yet commented on Washington’s decision. Read more: With the main opposition party suspended, Ecuador returns to the polls In light of the serious allegations, Loffredo said that cooperation has not completely ended: “We continue to work together to combat criminal structures.” He added that there are people who would like to see the recent military cooperation between Washington and Quito fall apart: “They want to damage these relationships that have yielded positive results, but we have a job to do, and the talks went very well.” The Trump administration has found in right-wing governments such as Noboa’s allies that support its foreign policy and reinforce its geopolitical project to reaffirm US hegemony over the West, a project embodied in the Shield of the Americas. The agreement signed by the vast majority of South American nations provides for the conduct of various military operations between the US military and the armed forces of each country to, as the agreement states, combat drug trafficking and terrorism anywhere on the American continent. For now, it is unclear what Washington’s decision will be if the allegations implicating Ecuadorian authorities in extrajudicial killings are proven true. What is certain is that the decision came at a politically inopportune time for Noboa, and it remains to be seen whether it will have significant immediate electoral consequences.
